summary: This note describes the tapetum lucidum, a reflective tissue layer behind the retina in many vertebrates and some other animals that acts as a retroreflector to boost night vision. It covers the optical mechanism, the four structural classes of tapeta and which animals have them, eyeshine and its colors, the red-eye effect in blue-eyed and heterochromatic cats and dogs, tapeta in spiders, human uses of eyeshine, artificial retroreflectors inspired by the structure, and drug-induced pathology in dogs.
one_line: Overview of the tapetum lucidum, the retroreflective eye layer that boosts night vision and produces eyeshine in many animals.
key_facts: The tapetum lucidum is a layer of tissue lying immediately behind the retina that acts as a retroreflector.
The tapetum lucidum reflects visible light back through the retina, increasing light available to photoreceptors while slightly blurring the image.
In the cat, the tapetum lucidum increases the sensitivity of vision by 44%.
Haplorhine primates, including humans, are diurnal and lack a tapetum lucidum.
The note classifies tapeta lucida into four types: retinal tapetum, choroidal guanine tapetum, choroidal tapetum cellulosum, and choroidal tapetum fibrosum.
Choroidal tapetum cellulosum is seen in carnivores, rodents and cetacea; dogs and ferrets use zinc, cats use riboflavin and zinc, and lemurs use only riboflavin.
Choroidal tapetum fibrosum is seen in cows, sheep, goats and horses and is an array of extracellular fibers, most commonly collagen.
Nathan H. Lents proposed that the tapetum lucidum evolved in vertebrates but not in cephalopods because of the backwards-facing nature of vertebrate photoreceptors.
Eyeshine occurs in colors including white, blue, green, yellow, pink and red, and its color varies with viewing angle and the minerals in the tapetum crystals.
Cats and dogs with blue eyes may display a distinctive red eyeshine in flash photographs, independent of the tapetum's eyeshine.
Most spider species have a tapetum located only in their smaller lateral eyes; the Salticidae have no tapetum.
Humans use scanning for reflected eyeshine, along with trained search dogs and search horses, to detect animals in the dark.
The Catseye brand raised pavement markers, the earliest artificial retroreflector patent, were inspired by the tapetum lucidum of a cat's eye.
In dogs, drugs including ethambutol, macrolide antibiotics, dithizone, and antimalarial medications can disturb tapetum crystal organization by chelating zinc from tapetal cells.
Reindeer tapetum color changes seasonally, helping them avoid predators in low-light winter at the cost of blurrier vision.

entities.name: Tapetum lucidum
entities.role: Layer of tissue behind the retina in the eye of many vertebrates that acts as a retroreflector and boosts night vision

entities.name: Nathan H. Lents
entities.role: American scientist who proposed the tapetum lucidum evolved in vertebrates but not cephalopods

entities.name: Catseye
entities.role: Brand of raised pavement markers whose earliest patent was inspired by the tapetum lucidum of a cat's eye

entities.name: Brownsnout spookfish
entities.role: Fish with an extraordinary focusing mirror derived from a retinal tapetum

entities.name: Aotus
entities.role: Neotropical night monkey genus sometimes described as having collagen-fibril tapetum but lacking riboflavin crystals

entities.name: Kākāpō
entities.role: Flightless bird that also possesses a tapetum lucidum
